analytic.title: Development of a Schedulability Analysis Framework based on pTPN and UPPAAL with Stopwatches

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.head: This
div.p: paper proposes an original schedulability framework which is based on preemptive Time Petri Nets (pTPNs) and UPPAAL with stopwatches (UPPAAL SW ). The realization enables a real-time tasking set, along with precedence constraints in the form of data control, message passing etc., to be uniformly formalized using pTPNs and then analyzed through model checking using UPPAAL SW in the presence of a reusable library of template processes modelling transitions of the source pTPNs specification and the scheduler algorithm which can be based on fixed priority or earliest deadline first. The paper first introduces and motivates the proposed approach by relating it to similar work described in literature, then summarizes the pTPNs formalism through a modelling example. After that the prototyped library in UPPAAL SW is presented and put to work for model checking the chosen real-time tasking set. Analysis of models which depend e.g. on non deterministic execution times and sporadic arrival times of tasks, is conditioned by the use of an over approximation in the generation of the model state graph.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: It is highly recognized that the use of formal methods is crucial both for the design and the verification of time critical systems. In the last years several tools have been proposed which permit, for example, a formal specification of a real-time system with time constraints, without preemption or suspension/resume mechanisms, and its thoroughly analysis through the generation and exploration of its associated model state graph. Popular formalisms include time-extended Petri nets, e.g. [1,2], and timed automata [3]. Analysis of a bounded system is decidable and depends on the concept of state classes for representing (hopefully) in finite terms the infinite behavior of the system which results from the adoption of a continuous time model which in turn implies dense firing times for transitions. A popular tool based on Time Petri Nets (TPNs) is TINA [4], whereas UPPAAL [5] is a widespread tool based on timed automata.

More realistic time-dependent systems may require task pre-emption for modelling the use of scarce resources (e.g. cpus) managed by a selected scheduling algorithm. Preemption is normally modelled by stopwatches, i.e. clocks which can be suspended and then resumed subsequently. Unfortunately, the use of stopwatches makes it the analysis to become undecidable in the general case. An over approximation of the reachability state space can then be generated [6] which can anyway guarantee the analysis process to be adequately carried out.

Preemptive Time Petri Nets (pTPNs) [7] extend TPNs with the concept of a timed transition which is statically tagged with a fixed priority value and a resource to be used for executing it. The firing time of such a transition can be suspended and later resumed from the point it was last left off. pTPNs are supported by the ORIS toolbox [8] which can enumerate state classes of a model under fixed-priority scheduling, using an over approximation technique. A key factor of ORIS is the possibility offered to the modeller of filtering out false behaviours in firing sequences thus allowing to find, in most cases, tight (best/worst) bounds in the execution time of a firing sequence (e.g. from the acquisition of a stimulus from the external environment to the generation of a response to it). In a recent paper [9] pTPNs are embedded in a system lifecycle which adheres to principles of regulatory standards for the construction of safety-critical software components.

The TIMESTOOL [10] embodies an extension of UPPAAL timed automata which permits modelling and analysis of systems running under preemptive scheduling. It allows one to compose timed automata with asynchronous tasks. However, the modelling language does not permit non deterministic execution times, the expression of dependencies among release and completion times of tasks, the use of multiple processing elements (cpus) for executing tasks.

The MoVES [11,12] framework enables an application decomposed in a collection of inter-dependent tasks to be mapped on to a execution platform consisting of different processing elements (PE) of a multiprocessor system-onchip. Each PE has local memory and is served by a real-time operating system. A bus structure with a given arbitration algorithm (e.g. FIFO based) is used to interconnect different PEs for data transfer. UPPAAL is used for task schedulability analysis (either under discrete time or by using stopwatches) and for memory and energy consumption of tasks.

A Model-based Framework for Schedulability Analysis (MFSA) based on UPPAAL equipped with stopwatches (UPPAAL WS ) was proposed in [13]. MFSA makes it possible to model preemptive systems under both fixed priority scheduling (FPS) or earliest deadline first (EDF) and enables the specification of precedence constraints by a directed acyclic graph where nodes denote tasks and dependencies are directed edges between nodes.

The novel approach proposed in this paper owes to both the pTPNs work and the MFSA schedulability analysis framework. pTPNs provide the basic modelling language which was adapted to work with not only FPS as in ORIS but also with EDF as in MFSA. A key difference from MFSA is that pTPNs can uniformly be exploited to specify both the task model structure and any required task dependencies. A reusable library of template processes was developed which reproduce in UPPAAL WS the semantics of pTPN preemptive transitions and that of the scheduling algorithm. Actually, the library includes template processes which can operate with preemptive/not preemptive FPS or EDF. The work described in this paper extends authors' previous work on schedulability analysis [14,15] which started by using integer clocks whose advancement is the responsibility of the modeller. Integer clocks, though, do not allow analysis of realistic pre-emptive tasking models.

The paper first introduces the pTPN formalism along with a tasking set example which can be difficult to analyze from the point of view of classical scheduling theory [16]. Then the current status of the catalog of developed UPPAAL WS templates which supports a structural translation from pTPNs to UPPAAL WS is illustrated. After that, the enabled model checking activities of pTPN models are demonstrated. Finally, conclusions are presented with an outlook to on-going and future work.

div.head: II. AN OVERVIEW OF PTPN MODELLING
div.p: Preemptive Time Petri Nets (pTPNs) [7] extend Time Petri Nets (TPN) [1]. In this work a Time Petri Net is defined as a tuple TPN=(P,T,B,F,I nh ,M 0 ,I s ) where:
• P and T are non empty and disjoint sets respectively of places and transitions of the underlying Petri net [17] • B is the backward incidence function: B:T×P→N, with N the set of natural numbers
• F is the forward incidence function: F:T×P→N
• I nh is a set of inhibitor arcs: I nh ⊆P×T • M 0 is the initial marking: M 0 :P→N in the usual sense of Petri nets
• I s is the static firing interval function, I s :T→N×(N∪{∞}).
A place p∈P is an input place for transition t if there is an arc with positive weight w from p to t, i.e. B(t,p)=w>0.

Similarly, p is an output place for t if there exists an arc from t to p with positive weight w, i.e. F(t,p)=w>0. Place p is an inhibitor place for transition t if (p,t)∈I nh , i.e. there exists an inhibitor arc connecting p to t. An inhibitor arc graphically ends with a small black circle. The set of input places of a transition is referred to as its preset. The set of output places of a transition constitutes its postset. In a similar way can be defined the preset and postset of a place. I s associates to each transition t a dense firing interval whose bounds are assumed to be specified by non negative integers: I s (t)=[a,b] with 0≤a≤b, b can be ∞. Bound a is said the earliest firing time (EFT) of t, b the latest firing time of t (LFT).

Transition enabling obeys to the same precondition on the input place tokens as in classical Petri nets. Transition firing semantics can be characterized by thinking about a timer (or clock) associated with a transition which is reset as soon as the transition gets enabled. Let τ be an instant in time when transition t is enabled. Provided t is continuously enabled, t cannot fire before τ+a but must fire (strong firing model) before or at τ+b, unless it is disabled by the firing of conflicting transition (race firing policy). Let θ be the elapsed time since τ as measured by the transition timer. The firing time t is τ+θ with a≤θ≤b. At transition firing, tokens are removed from the input places and new tokens are generated to output places as in classical Petri nets. As in [2], TPN transitions are assumed to be regulated by single server policy. A transition which is multiple enabled will fire its enablings one at a time. As a consequence, after its own firing, a still enabled transition is always regarded as a newly enabled one.

A pTPN is a tuple PTPN=(TPN,Res,Req,Prio) where Res is a set of resources (disjoint from T and P), Req associates each transition with a subset of Res, and Prio associates each transition with a natural number: Prio:T→N. The meaning of such a natural number depends on the scheduling algorithm. Under Fixed Priority Scheduling (FPS) it is the static priority assigned to the task to which the transition (i.e. computational step) belongs. Under Earliest Deadline First (EDF), the number expresses the (relative) task deadline. Distance to the deadline dynamically defines the task priority, i.e. of the computational step. An enabled preemptive transition can be in one of two states: in-progress or not-in-progress depending respectively if the associated resources (e.g. a cpu) are available or not. Progression status dictates if the underlying timer of the transition is allowed to advance or not toward the time to fire.

As shown in [7,9] pTPNs have the power for modelling general real-time embedded systems where tasks can possibly be allocated on multiple processors (e.g. multicore), can be periodic or sporadic and can have non deterministic execution times. In addition, task control structure may include mutual exclusion, precedence constraints and message-passing.

div.head: A. A tasking model set
div.p: Fig. 1 depicts a task model composed of three periodic task types T0, T2 and T3, and a sporadic task type T1. The example was adapted from [7] by converting, by a scale factor of 10, the bounds of static firing intervals of transitions, from rational numbers to natural values as required by UPPAAL WS . All tasks are ready at time 0. T0, T1 and T2 are supposed to be executed on the cpu1, whereas T3 runs on a distinct cpu2. The task set exhibits interaction on shared data between instances of T0 and T2, and instances of T0 and T3, guarded respectively by locks mutex1 and mutex2. A message passing mechanism exists between sporadic task T1 and periodic task T0. At each completion, task T1 sends a message to T0 by generating a token in the place p5. The behaviour of task T0 is modelled so as to process an available message in p5 (see the subnet t5p6t6) or to proceed without such a message (see transition t2 and inhibitor arc p5t2). Processing a message in p5 is carried out in critical section t6 guarded by mutex2. Fig. 1 witnesses a general benefit of pTPN modelling, namely the possibility of clearly specifying the internal control structure of each task type. Transitions t0, t7, t9, t14 are activating transitions respectively for the task types T0, T1, T2 and T3. At each firing of an activating transition, an instance of the corresponding task type is created (a token is deposited respectively in place p0, p4, p8, p13). The remaining transitions in each task are preemptive transitions which model computational steps of the task execution body.

Entering a critical section is modelled by an instantaneous transition (e.g. t5 vs. t16, or t3 vs. t11). Obviously, a priority inversion problem can occur when a low priority task enters its critical section just before the arrival of a high priority task running on the same cpu. For example, a priority inversion can occur between t4 and t12. Priority inversion problems can forbid schedulability, and can require an emulation of the priority ceiling protocol [16] to be adopted.

The model in Fig. 1 can easily be annotated to operate under EDF by replacing the priority number with the relative deadline of each task instance, which in a case can coincide with the period of the task type. Due to the combination of periodic/sporadic tasks, mutual exclusion, message passing and multiple processors, a task model like that in Fig. 1 can be impossible to analyze from the perspective of classic scheduling theory [16].

div.p: UPPAAL SW SUPPORTING PTPN A structural translation was defined for transforming a pTPN model into an equivalent network of UPPAAL WS timed automata (TA) or template processes. In the following only an informal argument about correctness of the translation will be given. The translation is assisted by an extension of the TPN-Designer toolbox [18] which permits a graphical drawing of a pTPN model, its preliminary behavioural checking through discrete event simulation, and its automated conversion to the terms of the UPPAAL WS library which is to be described. For brevity, only some fundamental template automata will be shown.

div.head: C. Activation transition automaton
div.p: This is a truly non preemptive Time Petri Nets (TPN) transition [1]. The automaton in Fig. 2 receives its transition ID, the belonging task id, and the relevant cpu id as parameters. It starts in the D (disabled) location. When enabled, the transition moves to the F (under firing) location, and resets its task clock x. The invariant of F states that the firing has to be completed within the upper bound of the transition time interval (the upper bound can be infinity).

At any time between the lower bound and the upper bound, the transition can terminate its firing by moving to the W (withdraw) location, provided it is still enabled. After that, the firing process completes by returning back to the D location, after having generated tokens in the postset places. Losing the enabledness status in F causes the transition to come back immediately to the D location. It should be noted that multiple enablings are served serially one at a time.

After its own firing, if a transition is still enabled, it is considered as new enabled (clock x starts again from 0). The proposed automaton coincides, except for the introduction of helper enabled(ID), withdraw(ID) and deposit(ID) global functions, with the TA proposed in [19] (see also [20]) where it is shown, by a formal proof based on a timed bisimulation, that the corresponding structural translation preserves the semantics of TPNs.

div.head: D. The Supervisor automaton
div.p: The supervisor automaton (see Fig. 3) is designed to step through the phases of the atomic firing process of any transition (activation or preemptive one) through a cycle S0-S1-S2-S3-S0. The cycle is started in the S0 location where the supervisor can allow an under firing transition to complete its firing, by launching a synchronization on the channel pre which causes a (non deterministically) chosen transition to perform its withdrawal phase. The intermediate marking vector M which follows a pre synchronization can enable/disable multiple transitions. Therefore an update broadcast signal is used which all transitions can hear in order to re-evaluate their statuses. After that the supervisor sends a post synchronization which triggers the deposit phase of the transition firing, followed by a second update broadcast which completes the firing process.

A transition which was enabled before pre, but then loses enabling after the first update is a non-persistent-transition (its firing is aborted). A transition which remains enabled during a whole execution cycle, is a persistent-transition. A transition which was disabled before pre, gets enabled during the cycle (after pre, and continue to be enabled after post or enables after post) is a newly-enabled-transition. The first update broadcast signal (see the edge from B to S0 in Fig. 3) serves to bootstrap a model, i.e. to allow transitions enabled in the model initial marking to reach the F location in Fig. 2 (or the NP or F location in Fig. 4).

div.head: E. Preemptive transition automaton
div.p: Fig. 4 portrays the developed automaton for a preemptive pTPN transition, which has the same parameters as for activation transition. It was achieved by decorating the automaton of the basic transition in Fig. 2 so as to be influenced by the decisions of a scheduler automaton. As soon as the transition gets enabled, it announces its arrival (function arrival() updates the request data structure) and goes into the choice point C1. Here the transition can move into F (progress location) or into NP (not-progressing location) depending on a decision of the scheduler. In the NP location the task clock is stopped (clock derivative is set to 0, i.e. x[taskId]'=0). From F (or NP) the transition is forced to re-evaluate its status following an update synchronization (which can correspond either to the withdrawal -preor deposit -postsub phase of a transition firing) sent by the supervisor. The transition then comes back to C1. Following a complete firing or an abort (e.g. see the edge from F to D), the transition signals its finishing (function finish() updates the request data structure).

The construction in Fig. 4 mirrors the design fact that it is useless to preempt a task (a transition) which has yet consumed all its computation time. Since in Petri nets two transitions which are up to conclude their firing at the same time, e.g. an activation transition which would start a new task instance and a preemptive transition which would finish its computational step (which can also be the last one in the task body) are handled non deterministically, the automaton in Fig. 4 purposely moves a preemptive transition to the FC location, through the committed choice point C2, thus freeing the task clock x, as x reaches the upper bound of the time interval, provided the transition is still enabled.

div.head: F. Preemptive scheduler automata
div.p: Template automata in Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 receive a cpu parameter at system configuration time. Simplicity of Fig. 5 stems from the fact that priority parameters are assigned statically and regulate the selection process of the FPS scheduler. The helper function requests() returns true if there are some task, on the cpu served by the scheduler, with a pending execution request. Function next(), provided there are some pending requests, returns the identity of a transition belonging to the (or one of) highest priority task. As one can see from Fig. 5 the Selection location is urgent, not committed, whereas locations S1, S2 and S3 of the supervisor (see Fig. 3) are committed (in UPPAAL, committed locations are always exited before urgent locations). This provision ensures current transition firing eventually terminates before the next decision of the scheduler is taken. Similarly, the choice point C1 was made urgent so as to give precedence to the scheduler next decision process.

Greater complexity in Fig. 6 (which in turn implies higher analysis cost) originates from the need of evaluating task priority dynamically, based on the distance from the task time (clock of the activation transition) to the task relative deadline. In addition, clock variables cannot be compared in the body of a function. Then the necessity of realizing loops directly on the model task structure through self-edges in Fig. 6. div.head: IV. SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS BY MODEL CHECKING
div.p: The extension of UPPAAL with stopwatches UPPAAL SW [6,13] offers an approximate reachability algorithm which reuses the existing efficient data-structures of the toolbox. The DBM-based algorithm of (UPPAAL SW ) yields an overapproximation (OA) of the reachable state space, which means that the zone component (firing domain or clock inequalities system) of a state class node of the state graph, can be larger than that required, for it to remain convex while coping with stopped clocks. OA influences the analysis by model checking in the following way. It is of no meaning checking for the reachability of a particular state, because such a state could be covered in a virtual subzone introduced by OA. An invariant property (e.g. a safety one), which is found satisfied in all the states of the state graph, obviously also hold on the original model. Nothing can be concluded, though, if an invariant property emerges that it may not be satisfiable under OA. In this case, in fact, the counter example which UPPAAL SW is capable of furnishing under OA, can possibly correspond to a false behaviour, i.e. to an impossible course of actions of the studied system. False behaviours can often be eliminated by relaxing a little the model timing constraints. It is worth noting, however, that, as demonstrated e.g. in [11,12], the reachability analysis enabled by UPPAAL SW is important from the practical point of view because it permits significant systems to be modelled and adequately analysed.

div.head: A. Schedulability of the example task model
div.p: A pTPN task model translated in UPPAAL SW according to the template library previously described, is schedulable if all the tasks meet their deadline in all the possible execution circumstances, which normally means they terminate within their assigned period. div.p: On the example task model under FPS, the verifier answers to the query (1) by saying that "Property may not be satisfied". It was found that a time interval of [103,INF] for the arrival of T1 sporadic process guarantees the query (1) to become satisfied. In another scenario, the model was checked by replacing the sporadic task by the (non equivalent) periodic process whose period coincides with the minimal interdistance between two consecutive arrivals, i.e. with the time interval [100,100].

In this worst case situation, query (1) was found satisfied. In addition, all the queries in Table 1 were found satisfied (it should be noted that schedulability of task T1 is already covered by query (1)). To emulate a priority ceiling protocol, transition t12 (see Fig. 1) can easily be annotated with the high priority 3 of the task T0. The results in Table 1, though, were confirmed with or without the provision for controlling the (potential) priority inversion problem between transition t4 and t12. Being schedulable, the response times of the four tasks were looked for by issuing queries like the following which refer to task T0:
div.formula: A[] t4.W imply time[task0]>=16 (2) A[] t4.W imply time[task0]<=43(3)
div.p: Such queries check the task time clock (i.e. the clock which governs the arrival time of the task) each time the preemptive transition t4 (the last one of T0) completes its firing (the automaton in Fig. 4 reaches the W location). The upper bound 16 and the lower bound 43 make it respectively the query (2) and (3) to be satisfied. A value less than 43, for example, causes the answer to query (3) to be "Property may not be satisfied". In the light of OA, it is not guaranteed that bounds in [16,43] are the tightest bounds (best case) BCRT, (worst case) WCRT of the T0 response time. Therefore, response times derived by queries as ( 2) and ( 3) are in general close estimations of their exact values. They, though, are very important for schedulability analysis, since if the worst case response times are lower than the task deadlines, the schedulability is guaranteed. Tables 2 reports the estimated task response times when FPS is adopted on both cpus. The experimental analysis was also devoted to checking multiprocessor "scheduling anomalies" known in the literature [21,11], which occur when interdependent processes run on distinct cpus. In these cases, early completion of a computation can change the relative starting time of computations on other processors. Two separate cases were studied: when transition t15 has a deterministic time interval corresponding to the lower bound ( [6,6]) and to the upper bound ( [12,12]) of its time interval. It emerged that the system (always using [100,100] for the arrival time of task T1) remains schedulable with the estimated response times of T0 which are respectively [16,39] and [16,33].

The model of Fig. 1 was also analyzed under EDF on both cpus, using as relative deadlines the task periods. The task model was found schedulable with the (non equivalent) periodic task [100,100] used instead of the sporadic task T1. The collected response times are as in the Table 3.

In another experimental scenario, the schedulability of the system model was checked when the two cpus adopt a different scheduler structure. The system was found schedulable and the task response times emerged as shown in Table 4 andTable 5.

Experiments were carried out on a Win 7, Intel Core i3, 2.13 GHz, 4GB, PC. Any query on the task model operated by FPS on both cpus lasts in a very few sec; it requires about 30 sec when EDF is run on both the processing elements. V. CONCLUSIONS The schedulability framework proposed in this paper represents an original and independent support of the Preemptive Time Petri Nets (pTPNs) formalism [7,9] on top of UPPAAL with stopwatches (UPPAAL SW ). The approach is flexible yet efficient.

Whereas in the ORIS tool [8] only a fixed priority scheduler is admitted, in the developed approach the scheduling policy can be customized. This paper shows a fixed priority scheduler automaton and one based on earliest deadline first, both preemptive in character. These schedulers were also adapted to work under a non preemptive scenario. In addition, a distinct scheduler algorithm can be associated to regulate the operation of each different processing element.

Although based on over-approximation, the schedulability analysis afforded by UPPAAL SW is very important in the practical use. As in [11,12] the adoption of non deterministic execution times for periodic tasks make it possible for UPPAAL SW to produce in many cases precise analysis results.
On-going and future work are directed to:
• Extending and improving the prototyped library, e.g. with the development of other scheduler automata.
• Experimenting with a redesign of the structural translation toward a reduction in the number of clocks (e.g. by using one automaton with one clock for controlling the arrivals of tasks).
• Using the framework for the schedulability analysis of realistic industrial real-time system models.
• Defining a whole methodology for the formal modelling, analysis and development of embedded systems over multiprocessor system-on-chips (MPSoC) [9,11,12].

I[ID][0] is the static lower bound of the time interval of transition ID, I[ID][1] is the upper bound of the static time interval. The upper bound can be INF. The contents of these matrixes are constant and do not contribute to the memory size of a state class node of the model state graph. The marking vector of a pTPN model is represented by the vector: int M[P]={...};
